subject: 2 papers on efficient covariance matrix estimation

messages.author: da33143a8db60ce8
messages.subject: 2 papers on efficient covariance matrix estimation
parts:
Hi all.  I met this guy Xi Luo today who was telling me about this (non-Bayesian) regularization approach he had for estimating covariance matrices.  Could this be relevant for us?  I could think of various Stan connections:
- Estimating a mass matrix for Nuts
- A faster way to do “lmer”-type models
- Maybe there’s a Bayesian version of this model that could make sense for us.

Michael, Ben, Marcus (or anyone else):  What do you think?

See you
A

messages.author: a5e83218c834e013
messages.subject: Re: 2 papers on efficient covariance matrix estimation
parts:
Is there any novelty here that’s not related to sparse estimation?  In particular
the L1 regularization won’t have the same utility for a Bayesian model because
of the inability to explicitly remove a coefficient from the model.  Sparse metrics
might be a useful bridge between diagonal and dense metrics depending if the
sparsity pattern manifests in faster Cholesky factorizations (I’m not up on the
sparse Cholesky stuff these days but my impression is that it’s not typically
helpful).

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] 2 papers on efficient covariance matrix estimation
parts:
Hi, yes, I’m not sure, I think one reason for preferring sparse matrices is for computation as you say, but another reason is that the estimates in these papers are highly regularlized, which addresses the issue that simple estimates of cov matrices tend to be noisy.
A

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] 2 papers on efficient covariance matrix estimation
parts:
I think Andrew's proposing estimating the mass matrix this way,
not a posterior somewhere.

There are a gazillion papers out there on low-rank matrix
estimation in the specific context of covariance. Martin
Wainwright gave a nice departmental seminar a year or two ago
on a mixture sparsity prior of what I recall to be a low-rank
approximation and a heavily L1-regularized approximation.

For some problems, you actually know some of the sparsity structure
in advance, so you can optimize there.

- Bob
